\section{Core Architectural Elements of the Information View}

\subsection{Information Structure and Content}

The Human Benchmark system's information structure centers around several key data entities that are fundamental to its operation. Rather than detailing every attribute, this view focuses on the architecturally significant entities and their relationships.

\subsubsection{Key Data Entities}

Note this diagram only shows the new data entities that will be created to implement the new feature and those that are closley related, but whose purpose is not clear(The User entity is not shown, etc.). The diagram uses Crowfoot notation for ER diagrams.
Only a diagram for the static model is shown, as such the information flow model and information lifecycle model will be described by text as they are extremly trivial. Other models such as volumetric, metadata, information quality and information ownership will not be covered as they are not relevant to chats or it is obvious as for what kind of model is used due to the nature of the change being implemented(The owner of a message is its sender, the identifier for all data is it's id, etc.).

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Emojis}: Stores all emojis and messages that have these emojis.
    \item \textbf{Files}: Stores all of the files and a link to the message to which the file is attached.
    \item \textbf{GameRoomMessages}: This entity shows the messages that were sent to game rooms.
    \item \textbf{PrivateMessages}: This entity contains all messages that were sent in private chats.
    \item \textbf{Groups}: This entity stores all of the chat-groups that were created by users.
    \item \textbf{GroupMessages}: All of the messages sent to chat-groups.
    \item \textbf{GlobalMessages}: All of the messages that were sent in the global scope.
    \item \textbf{GameSessions}: All of the currently running game sessions(Used by game-room messages to store in which game-room the message was sent).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Information Storage Model}
The data will be stored in a relational database. This is because they are widely used and have a way to unsure their quality such as the various normal forms and SQL.

\subsection{Information Flow}


\subsubsection{Real-time Communication Flows}

% Since there are no system messages that use the chatting system, the data flow is as follows: the user sends a message which is sent to the real-time communication system which according to what kind of message it is it is forwarded to be sent to all users connected to the apropriate chat room and it is forwarded to the database for storage.

\begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{AutomationAndSections/Sections/3informationView/Image/infoFlow.png}
    \caption{Information Flow Diagram}
    \label{fig:information_flow_diagram}
\end{figure}

Our system lets users play reaction-time games, compete in multiplayer, and
track scores. When you interact with the app (like logging in, clicking targets,
or chatting), the frontend (React) sends requests to the backend (ASP.NET API).
The backend saves your data (scores, settings, messages) in a PostgreSQL
database and handles real-time multiplayer using WebSockets. Finally, the
frontend updates instantly to show leaderboards, game targets, and chat messages
based on the backend’s responses.

\subsection{Information lifecycles}

% The messages can have the following states. There are two states that a message
% may have. Firstly a message may be pinned. This state is reversable, as in once
% a message has been pinned and its state has changed to pinned it can also be
% unpinned and the state of the message will revert. The second state that a
% message can have is the deleted state. Since our system does not delete messages
% by default the only way messages are deleted is following a users request to
% delete them.

\begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{AutomationAndSections/Sections/3informationView/Image/messagelifecycle.png}
    \caption{Message Lifecycle Diagram}
    \label{fig:message_lifecycle_diagram}
\end{figure}

We use this flow to describe how a message lives and moves through our system.
It all starts when a message is created, triggered by either a global or
room-specific event. Once created, global messages are saved to the database,
while room messages are kept temporarily in memory. From there, messages can be
retrieved either through HTTP calls or WebSocket broadcasts, handled by our
services. After retrieval, they’re shown in the chat UI for users to see. Older
global messages are archived in the database, and room messages are removed from
memory when no longer needed, like when a room closes or the server restarts.
Eventually, all messages reach an end state when they’re no longer displayed or
stored.

\subsection{Information Ownership Model}


\begin{table}[H]
    \centering
    \caption{Information Ownership Model}
    \label{tab:ownership}
    \begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
        \hline
                                    & \textbf{User} & \textbf{Game} & \textbf{Score} & \textbf{Target} & \textbf{Message} & \textbf{Room} \\
        \hline
        \textbf{AuthService}        & Owner         & None          & None           & None            & None             & None          \\
        \textbf{GameService}        & Reader        & Owner         & Creator        & Owner           & None             & None          \\
        \textbf{MultiplayerService} & Reader        & Reader        & Creator        & Reader          & None             & Owner         \\
        \textbf{MessageService}     & Reader        & None          & None           & None            & Owner            & Reader        \\
        \textbf{LeaderboardService} & Reader        & Reader        & Reader         & None            & None             & None          \\
        \hline
    \end{tabular}
\end{table}

The table above shows the ownership model for the Human Benchmark system.
Read the table as follows: the services on the left show what kind of access they have to the data on the top.

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Owner}: Full control (create, read, update, delete).
    \item \textbf{Creator}: Can only create new entries (no updates/deletes).
    \item \textbf{Reader}: Can only view data (no changes).
    \item \textbf{None}: No access to this data.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Example:} AuthService is the Owner of User data (can register/edit/delete users), while LeaderboardService is just a Reader (can view scores but not modify them).

        Accessibility                      & \greencircle Low     & The information object connected to the real-time messaging functionality is not related to accessibility from an architectural perspective.        \\

        Availability and Resilience        & \redcircle High      & Since we are implementing chatting in real time it is important that upon a users request old messages are loaded and new ones created effectively. \\

        Development Resource               & \yellowcircle Medium & The database and information management implementation requires consideration of development effort.                                                \\

        Evolution                          & \greencircle Low     & The messages that will be created have little to no need to change over time.                                                                       \\

        Internationalization               & \greencircle Low     & The Internationalization of chats is depend on users and users alone. There is no architectural way or need to Internationalize messages.           \\



        Security                           & \greencircle Low     & User messages have little to no need to have security measures in place for users.                                                                  \\

        Usability                          & \greencircle Low     & While usability is important for the system overall, it has limited direct impact on the underlying information model.                              \\

    \end{tabular}
